claim: The simultaneous application of PET and MRI has revolutionized the ability to assess brain function across various physiological dimensions.
source: The simultaneous application of PET and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has revolutionized our ability to assess brain function across various physiological dimensions (Wehrl et al., 2013; Judenhofer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wehrl et al., 2013 and Judenhofer et al., 2008

claim: Combining PET with fMRI has opened many investigative avenues.
source: Combining PET with fMRI has opened many investigative avenues.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of multimodal imaging capabilities

claim: Resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) is a technique used in neuroscience.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biswal et al., 1995

claim: Pharmacological MRI (phMRI) is a technique used in neuroscience.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jonckers et al., 2015

claim: PET can quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability.
source: Techniques such as resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) (Biswal et al., 1995) or pharmacological MRI (phMRI) (Jonckers et al., 2015) are now complemented by the ability of PET to quantify molecular changes, including alterations in receptor and transporter availability (Sander et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sander et al., 2013

claim: The BOLD signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling.
source: The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling (Buxton, 2012), revealing only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buxton, 2012

claim: The BOLD signal reveals only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
source: The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in fMRI indirectly captures neuronal changes through neurovascular coupling (Buxton, 2012), revealing only the hemodynamic consequences of molecular-level drug effects.
evidence: Based on understanding of BOLD signal limitations

claim: PET has been used mainly in pharmacological studies to illustrate quantitative shifts in neuroreceptor or transporter availability.
source: Typically, PET, used independently or simultaneously with fMRI, has been used mainly in pharmacological studies to illustrate quantitative shifts in neuroreceptor or transporter availability (Silberbauer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Silberbauer et al., 2019

claim: Several studies have explored the interregional coherence of PET tracer signals.
source: Several studies have also explored the interregional coherence of PET tracer signals (Amend et al., 2019; Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017), an approach akin to fMRI-derived rs-FC.
evidence: Supported by citations to Amend et al., 2019; Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017

claim: Subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals.
source: While subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals (Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019), studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans (Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019

claim: Studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans.
source: While subject-level metabolic connectivity using [18F]FDG-PET has been established through the temporal correlation of regional PET signals (Wehrl et al., 2013; Amend et al., 2019), studies employing transporter or receptor tracers have focused predominantly on interregional binding coherence across subjects using static scans (Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017

claim: The concept and feasibility of molecular connectivity (MC) through the temporal correlation of the dynamic binding potentials of transporter or receptor tracers has yet to be explored.
source: The concept and feasibility of molecular connectivity (MC) (Hahn et al., 2019; Sala et al., 2023) through the temporal correlation of the dynamic binding potentials of transporter or receptor tracers has yet to be explored.
evidence: Statement of research gap in the literature

claim: The study investigated the feasibility of deriving MC from dynamic [11C]DASB-PET scans acquired simultaneously with fMRI in rats.
source: In our study, we investigated the feasibility of deriving MC from dynamic [11C]DASB-PET scans acquired simultaneously with fMRI in rats.
evidence: Direct statement of study objective

claim: The rats were divided into two cohorts: a baseline group and a pharmacological application group exposed to MDMA.
source: We divided the rats into two cohorts, a baseline group and a pharmacological application group, which were exposed to 3,4-methylenedeoxymetamphetamine (MDMA).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: There is a moderate but significant correlation between edge-level MC and FC (r=0.51, p<0.001).
source: We found a moderate but significant correlation between the edge-level MC and FC (r=0.51, p<0.001; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Statistical analysis result with reference to Figure 1A and B

claim: Both MC and FC connectomes revealed small-world properties at the group level, with coefficients higher than 1.
source: Furthermore, both connectomes revealed small-world properties at the group level, with coefficients higher than 1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Graph theory analysis result with reference to Figure 1C

claim: At the subject level, three molecular and four functional connectomes fell below the threshold of 1 for the small-world coefficient.
source: At the subject level, three molecular and four functional connectomes fell below the threshold of 1 for the small-world coefficient.
evidence: Subject-level analysis result

claim: FC showed higher consistency between early and late scan-derived connectomes (r=0.96) compared to MC (r=0.8).
source: Significant consistency was observed between early and late scan-derived connectomes (Figure 1D for FC, G for MC), with FC having a slight edge (Figure 1E, r=0.96) over MC (Figure 1H, r=0.8).
evidence: Temporal stability analysis with reference to Figures 1D, E, G, and H

claim: Ten group independent components were extracted from the fMRI data, revealing known canonical resting-state networks.
source: We extracted ten group ICs from the fMRI data (Figure 2A), revealing known canonical resting-state networks, such as the posterior default-mode-like network (IC1-5, red), sensorimotor networks (IC1-5, green and purple), the anterior default-mode-like network (IC6-10, yellow) and the visual network (IC6-10, red).
evidence: ICA results with reference to Figure 2A

claim: Two independent components were initially extracted from MC data, with IC1 comprising subcortical and cortical anterior brain regions and IC2 comprising deeper posterior areas.
source: Given the unpredictability of the number of ICs suitable for MC IC extraction, we started with two components (Figure 2B). IC1 (orange) comprised both subcortical and cortical anterior brain regions, including the nucleus accumbens, amygdala, cingulate cortex, caudate putamen, orbitofrontal cortex and medial prefrontal cortex, whereas IC2 (blue) primarily received contributions from deeper posterior areas, such as the midbrain, thalamus, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray cortex and medulla.
evidence: ICA results with reference to Figure 2B

claim: When 10 independent components were extracted from MC data, the initial anterior component split into four different ICs and the initial posterior IC split into three different ICs.
source: Interestingly, when we extracted 10 independent components to mimic the number of components used for the FC data, the initial anterior component split into four different ICs, and the initial posterior IC split into three different ICs.
evidence: ICA results with different component numbers

claim: MDMA induced immediate strong decreases in all SERT subcortical network regions, while salience areas exhibited a delay of approximately 10 min.
source: Interestingly, MDMA induced immediate strong decreases in all SERT subcortical network regions, and salience areas exhibited a delay of approximately 10 min (Figure 3A).
evidence: Temporal analysis of MDMA effects with reference to Figure 3A

claim: There is a highly significant correlation between the z scores of the posterior and anterior ICs and the t scores of late and early MDMA effects on [11C]DASB alterations (p<0.001).
source: To quantify the striking spatial similarity between the baseline independent components and the spatiotemporal characteristics of [11C]DASB changes after MDMA exposure, we found highly significant correlations between the z scores of the posterior and anterior ICs and the t scores of late and early MDMA effects on [11C]DASB alterations (p<0.001, Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reference to Figure 3C

claim: The decreases in MC and [11C]DASB BPND following MDMA application showed only a low correlation (r=0.29).
source: We found that the decreases in MC and [11C]DASB BPND following MDMA application (Figure 4A) showed only a low correlation (r=0.29, Figure 4B).
evidence: Correlation analysis with reference to Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Decreases in SERT availability exhibited a strong anterior-posterior gradient, most pronounced in areas with high SERT availability.
source: While decreases in SERT availability exhibited a strong anterior-posterior gradient, which was most pronounced in areas with high SERT availability, such as the MB, VTA, Pons, or PAG, the MC encompassed regions across the brain to similar extents.
evidence: Spatial pattern analysis of MDMA effects

claim: A 16% decrease in salience network FC was observed at the end of the scan after MDMA (p=0.02, did not survive FDR correction).
source: We observed a decrease in SN FC (16% at the end of the scan, p=0.02, did not survive FDR correction) and almost constant FC of the subcortical network (<5% decrease, p=0.79) following MDMA, as shown in Figure 5A at the edge and node levels and Figure 5C at the network level.
evidence: Statistical analysis of FC changes with reference to Figures 5A and 5C

claim: Almost constant FC of the subcortical network was observed following MDMA (<5% decrease, p=0.79).
source: We observed a decrease in SN FC (16% at the end of the scan, p=0.02, did not survive FDR correction) and almost constant FC of the subcortical network (<5% decrease, p=0.79) following MDMA, as shown in Figure 5A at the edge and node levels and Figure 5C at the network level.
evidence: Statistical analysis of FC changes with reference to Figures 5A and 5C

claim: Profound reductions in the subcortical network MC were observed following MDMA (p=0.009).
source: For MC, we observed profound reductions in the subcortical network (Figure 5C and D, p=0.009), emphasizing the acute and spatially specific effect of MDMA on MC.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MC changes with reference to Figures 5C and 5D

claim: [11C]DASB binding reflects the interplay of serotonin levels and SERT dynamics.
source: Our findings suggest that [11C]DASB binding reflects the interplay of serotonin levels and SERT dynamics (Paterson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paterson et al., 2010

claim: Evidence indicates that endogenous serotonin competes with tracers for binding sites, affecting tracer binding.
source: In support of the competition model, evidence indicates that endogenous serotonin competes with tracers for binding sites, affecting tracer binding (Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamamoto et al., 2007

claim: Contrasting results from various studies highlight the complexity of the interaction between serotonin and tracer binding.
source: However, contrasting results from various studies highlight the complexity of this interaction (Lundquist et al., 2007; Talbot et al., 2005; Lefevre et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lundquist et al., 2007; Talbot et al., 2005; Lefevre et al., 2017

claim: The internalization model suggests that serotonin levels influence SERT internalization, impacting [11C]DASB binding.
source: The internalization model suggests that serotonin levels influence SERT internalization, impacting [11C]DASB binding (Paterson et al., 2010; Ramamoorthy and Blakely, 1999; Blakely et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paterson et al., 2010; Ramamoorthy and Blakely, 1999; Blakely et al., 1998

claim: Some models have proposed a regulatory function of the raphé nuclei in maintaining serotonin fluctuations over several temporal scales at rest.
source: Some models on this topic have proposed a regulatory function of the raphé nuclei in maintaining serotonin fluctuations over several temporal scales at rest (Salomon and Cowan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salomon and Cowan, 2013

claim: Fast microdialysis has resolved multiple spontaneous surges of up to 1500-fold of the basal serotonin occurring during 30 min intervals.
source: Remarkably, fast microdialysis has resolved multiple spontaneous surges of up to 1500-fold of the basal serotonin occurring during 30 min intervals (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013

claim: SERT expression is essential for spontaneous serotonin surges and reduced SERT drastically decreases serotonin spiking.
source: Additionally, the same study indicated that SERT expression is essential for spontaneous surges and that reduced SERT drastically decreases serotonin spiking.
evidence: Inference from Yang et al., 2013 study

claim: SERT regulation occurs over multiple time scales, ranging from milliseconds to hours, depending on the mechanism involved.
source: In addition, SERT regulation occurs over multiple time scales, ranging from milliseconds to hours, depending on the mechanism involved (Lau and Schloss, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lau and Schloss, 2012

claim: Rapid changes in SERT surface expression can be mediated by protein-protein interactions or posttranslational modifications.
source: Rapid changes in SERT surface expression can be mediated by protein-protein interactions or posttranslational modifications (Jayanthi et al., 2005; Steiner et al., 2008), such as phosphorylation, which occur on a timescale of milliseconds to minutes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jayanthi et al., 2005; Steiner et al., 2008

claim: The graph theory analysis revealed comparable whole-brain organization between the hemodynamic (BOLD-derived) and serotonergic (PET-derived) connectomes.
source: Our graph theory analysis revealed comparable whole-brain organization between the hemodynamic (BOLD-derived) and serotonergic (PET-derived) connectomes, although we found only a moderate correlation between the edges of the two measurements.
evidence: Graph theory analysis results

claim: The [11C]DASB-based MC results showed a distinct binding pattern compared with BOLD-fMRI-derived FC.
source: Notably, the [11C]DASB-based MC results showed a distinct binding pattern compared with BOLD-fMRI-derived FC.
evidence: Comparison of imaging modalities

claim: For FC, the ICA revealed classic RSNs, including the default-mode network, sensory network, and motor network, consistent with previous studies in rats and humans.
source: For FC, the ICA revealed classic RSNs, including the default-mode network, sensory network, and motor network, consistent with previous studies in rats (Becerra et al., 2011) and humans (Fox et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Becerra et al., 2011 and Fox et al., 2005

claim: The PET data revealed two distinct anatomical components in the serotonergic system: one including key subcortical areas and another comprising regions of the limbic system.
source: In contrast, the PET data revealed two distinct anatomical components in the serotonergic system. One component included key subcortical areas, such as the brainstem, parts of the midbrain, and the thalamus, regions rich in SERT availability and central to serotonergic regulation. The other component comprised regions of the limbic system, such as the striatum, amygdala, insula, cingulate cortex, and prefrontal cortex, critical targets of serotonergic projections from the raphe nuclei.
evidence: ICA analysis of PET data

claim: PET ICs appeared less bilateral than fMRI ICs, likely due to the lower temporal resolution of PET.
source: In our analysis, PET ICs appeared less bilateral than fMRI ICs. This is likely due to the lower temporal resolution of PET (80 frames) than of fMRI (2400 frames), resulting in a reduced signal‒to‒noise ratio (SNR) and potentially affecting the stability and symmetry of the independent components.
evidence: Inference based on technical differences between imaging modalities

claim: MDMA induces more pronounced changes in MC compared with FC, particularly in regions associated with the SERT subcortical network.
source: Our results demonstrate that compared with FC, MDMA induces more pronounced changes in MC, particularly in regions associated with the SERT subcortical network.
evidence: Comparison of MDMA effects on MC and FC

claim: The distinct temporal dynamics of BPND variations between components may reflect the hierarchical organization of the serotonergic system.
source: The distinct temporal dynamics of BPND variations between these components may reflect the hierarchical organization of the serotonergic system.
evidence: Interpretation of temporal dynamics data

claim: The raphe nuclei are likely to exert more immediate modulation on posterior subcortical structures (IC2), whereas downstream effects on limbic and cortical regions (IC1) may occur more gradually.
source: Specifically, the raphe nuclei, as the primary source of serotonin, are likely to exert more immediate modulation on posterior subcortical structures (IC2), whereas downstream effects on limbic and cortical regions (IC1) may occur more gradually.
evidence: Speculation based on neuroanatomical knowledge

claim: Previous studies evaluating the effects of MDMA on FC have indicated relatively few effects on FC.
source: Previous studies evaluating the effects of MDMA on FC have indicated relatively few effects on FC (Carhart-Harris et al., 2015; Roseman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carhart-Harris et al., 2015; Roseman et al., 2014

claim: The findings align with Salvan et al., 2023, who integrated molecular maps into fMRI data and demonstrated how individual serotonergic receptors contribute to network-level activity.
source: Our findings align with Salvan et al., 2023, who integrated molecular maps into fMRI data and demonstrated how individual serotonergic receptors contribute to network-level activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Salvan et al., 2023

claim: Dipasquale et al. reported that MDMA specifically decreased FC in the 5HT1A maps in areas that could be ascribed to the human salience network.
source: The dual regression approach reported by Salvan et al. was first reported in the context of pharmacology to delineate the receptor-specific effects of MDMA in humans (Dipasquale et al., 2019). The authors found that MDMA specifically decreased FC in the 5HT1A maps in areas that could be ascribed to the human salience network, such as the insula and a collection of medial cortical regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dipasquale et al., 2019

claim: A trend towards reduced salience FC and MC was observed in the data, though not reaching significance.
source: While not reaching significance, we observed a trend towards reduced salience FC and MC in our data.
evidence: Statistical trend in the data

claim: Over the past decade, PET studies using [11C]DASB have focused on the associations of SERT availability across different brain regions.
source: Over the past decade, PET studies using [11C]DASB have focused on the associations of serotonin transporter (SERT) availability across different brain regions, revealing altered interregional SERT connections in patient cohorts, posttreatment changes, and a predictive capacity for treatment response (Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017; James et al., 2017; Hahn et al., 2014; Hahn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanzenberger et al., 2012; Vanicek et al., 2017; James et al., 2017; Hahn et al., 2014; Hahn et al., 2010

claim: The study reveals significant within-subject temporal associations in [11C]DASB binding.
source: Our study builds upon this foundation, revealing significant within-subject temporal associations in [11C]DASB binding and demonstrates more pronounced alterations in MC than in FC induced by drugs, thus highlighting the enhanced utility of our method.
evidence: Study findings

claim: The study demonstrates more pronounced alterations in MC than in FC induced by drugs.
source: Our study builds upon this foundation, revealing significant within-subject temporal associations in [11C]DASB binding and demonstrates more pronounced alterations in MC than in FC induced by drugs, thus highlighting the enhanced utility of our method.
evidence: Comparison of MC and FC changes

claim: The experimental protocols predate the recently published consensus recommendations for rat fMRI.
source: One limitation of our study is that our experimental protocols predate the recently published consensus recommendations for rat fMRI (Grandjean et al., 2023), particularly concerning anesthesia and preprocessing pipelines.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation with citation to Grandjean et al., 2023

claim: Isoflurane at 1.3% maintains stable physiological parameters and avoids burst suppression.
source: However, we previously demonstrated that isoflurane at 1.3% maintains stable physiological parameters and avoids burst suppression (Ionescu et al., 2021b), a concern at higher doses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ionescu et al., 2021b

claim: Low-dose isoflurane remains feasible for resting-state functional connectivity studies.
source: Furthermore, other studies have reported that low-dose isoflurane remains feasible for resting-state functional connectivity studies (Hutchison et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hutchison et al., 2014

claim: The number of animals used for the pharmacological study with MDMA was low compared to the resting-state cohort.
source: Additionally, the number of animals used for our pharmacological study with MDMA was low compared to the resting-state cohort.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation

claim: The consistency of effects between subjects indicated in the data points towards the stability of results even at the employed group size.
source: While future studies with higher group sizes may be valuable to confirm and expand our findings, the consistency of effects between subjects indicated in our data points towards the stability of our results even at the employed group size.
evidence: Interpretation of data consistency

claim: At rest, MC data are reliable, temporally stable, and exhibit similar graph theory metrics to traditionally calculated functional connectomes.
source: First, we show that at rest, the data are reliable, temporally stable, and exhibit similar graph theory metrics to traditionally calculated functional connectomes.
evidence: Summary of baseline findings

claim: Despite comparable network-level organizational properties, at rest, MC is only moderately correlated with FC.
source: Second, despite comparable network-level organizational properties, at rest, MC is only moderately correlated with FC, indicating the complementary nature of both readouts.
evidence: Comparison of MC and FC

claim: Resting-state MC ICs correlate well with SERT occupancy changes induced by the MDMA challenge.
source: Third, resting-state MC ICs correlate well with SERT occupancy changes induced by the MDMA challenge.
evidence: Correlation analysis between baseline and MDMA effects

claim: Changes in BPND are more pronounced in regions with higher baseline SERT availabilities.
source: Our data indicate that while changes in BPND are more pronounced in regions with higher baseline SERT availabilities, MC reveals a more globally distributed measure of tracking serotonergic changes since regions, such as the insula, with relatively low SERT expression, are strongly affected.
evidence: Comparison of BPND and MC changes

claim: MC reveals a more globally distributed measure of tracking serotonergic changes compared to BPND.
source: Our data indicate that while changes in BPND are more pronounced in regions with higher baseline SERT availabilities, MC reveals a more globally distributed measure of tracking serotonergic changes since regions, such as the insula, with relatively low SERT expression, are strongly affected.
evidence: Comparison of spatial patterns of BPND and MC changes

claim: The multimodal imaging approach cannot fully decipher the mechanisms of interregional coherence in PET time courses.
source: However, our multimodal imaging approach, although powerful, cannot fully decipher the mechanisms of interregional coherence in PET time courses.
evidence: Acknowledgment of methodological limitation

claim: Subject-level MC are reliable and complementary to FC in both resting and pharmacologically challenged states.
source: This study significantly contributes to integrating molecular data into connectomic frameworks, demonstrating that subject-level MC are reliable and complementary to FC in both resting and pharmacologically challenged states.
evidence: Summary of study contributions

claim: A total of 41 male Lewis rats were obtained from Charles River Laboratories.
source: A total of 41 male Lewis rats were obtained from Charles River Laboratories (Sulzfeld, Germany).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: Thirty rats underwent baseline [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans without any pharmacological intervention.
source: Thirty rats (354±37 g, corresponding to 11 wk of age) underwent baseline [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans without any pharmacological intervention, whereas 11 rats (365±19 g, corresponding to 11 wk of age) underwent [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans, including an acute MDMA challenge.
evidence: Description of experimental groups

claim: Eleven rats underwent [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans including an acute MDMA challenge.
source: Thirty rats (354±37 g, corresponding to 11 wk of age) underwent baseline [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans without any pharmacological intervention, whereas 11 rats (365±19 g, corresponding to 11 wk of age) underwent [11C]DASB PET/fMRI scans, including an acute MDMA challenge.
evidence: Description of experimental groups

claim: All experiments were in compliance with German federal regulations for experimental animals and received approval from the Regierungspräsidium Tübingen.
source: All experiments were in compliance with German federal regulations for experimental animals and received approval from the Regierungspräsidium Tübingen.
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance

claim: The rats were subjected to simultaneous PET/fMRI experiments involving 1.3% isoflurane anesthesia.
source: The rats were subjected to simultaneous PET/fMRI experiments involving 1.3% isoflurane anesthesia, tail vein catheterization, positioning on a temperature-controlled bed, and monitoring of vital signs.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: The scans were performed using a 7T small-animal ClinScan MRI scanner with a custom-developed PET insert.
source: The scans were performed using a 7T small-animal ClinScan MRI scanner (Bruker Biospin, Ettlingen, Germany) with a custom-developed PET insert (Disselhorst et al., 2022).
evidence: Description of imaging equipment with citation to Disselhorst et al., 2022

claim: For [11C]DASB PET, a bolus plus constant infusion protocol (kbol = 38.7 min) was employed.
source: For [11C]DASB PET, we employed a bolus plus constant infusion protocol (kbol = 38.7 min) and reconstructed the scans in 1 min time frames.
evidence: Description of PET protocol

claim: The MDMA cohort received a pharmacological MDMA challenge of 3.2 mg/kg intravenously 40 min after tracer injection.
source: The MDMA cohort received a pharmacological MDMA challenge of 3.2 mg/kg intravenously 40 min after tracer injection.
evidence: Description of MDMA administration protocol

claim: Data preprocessing followed established protocols, including realignment, mask creation, coregistration, spatial normalization, signal cleaning, and spatial smoothing.
source: Data preprocessing followed established protocols, including steps such as realignment, mask creation, coregistration, spatial normalization, signal cleaning, and spatial smoothing, as detailed in our previous work (Ionescu et al., 2023).
evidence: Description of preprocessing methods with citation to Ionescu et al., 2023

claim: For the MDMA dataset, PET scans were analyzed for early and late effects post-challenge using the general linear model (GLM) available in SPM.
source: For the MDMA dataset, PET scans were analyzed for early and late effects post-challenge using the general linear model (GLM) available in SPM.
evidence: Description of analysis method

claim: The baseline was defined as 30–40 min after the start of the scan for both datasets.
source: For both datasets, the baseline was defined as 30–40 min after the start of the scan.
evidence: Definition of baseline period

claim: Static PET scans were generated by summing dynamic frames over defined periods for 10 min periods after the MDMA challenge.
source: Static PET scans were generated by summing dynamic frames over defined periods for 10 min periods after the MDMA challenge (50–60 min to investigate early effects and 70–80 min to investigate late MDMA effects).
evidence: Description of static PET scan generation

claim: FC was determined using a seed-based analysis approach.
source: FC was determined using a seed-based analysis approach.
evidence: Description of FC analysis method

claim: Pairwise Pearson's correlation coefficients were calculated between each pair of mean regional time series for every dataset.
source: Pairwise Pearson's correlation coefficients were calculated between each pair of mean regional time series for every dataset.
evidence: Description of correlation analysis

claim: The Pearson's r coefficients were converted into z values using Fischer's transformation for group-level analysis.
source: The Pearson's r coefficients were converted into z values using Fischer's transformation for group-level analysis.
evidence: Description of statistical transformation

claim: Binding potentials were calculated framewise for all dynamic PET scans using the DVR-1 to generate regional BPND values with the cerebellar gray matter as a reference region.
source: Binding potentials were calculated framewise for all dynamic PET scans using the DVR-1 (Equation 1) to generate regional BPND values with the cerebellar gray matter as a reference region, which our earlier studies demonstrated to be the most appropriate for this tracer in rats (Walker et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2020)
evidence: Description of binding potential calculation with citations to Walker et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2020

claim: The first 20 min of every scan were discarded, which were dominated by perfusion effects.
source: To calculate the MC, we discarded the first 20 min of every scan, which were dominated by perfusion effects, and applied a detrending approach to the remaining 60 min to obtain temporally stable values (for further details, please refer to the Supplementary Methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of data processing for MC calculation

claim: A detrending approach was applied to the remaining 60 min to obtain temporally stable values for MC calculation.
source: To calculate the MC, we discarded the first 20 min of every scan, which were dominated by perfusion effects, and applied a detrending approach to the remaining 60 min to obtain temporally stable values (for further details, please refer to the Supplementary Methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of detrending procedure

claim: Group ICA was used for ICA in the baseline group using the GIFT toolbox.
source: Group ICA (GIFT toolbox, MIALAB, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA) was used for ICA in the baseline group.
evidence: Description of ICA method and software

claim: For fMRI, ten independent components were selected, while two components were initially selected for PET.
source: For fMRI, we selected ten independent components, while we started with two components for PET and increased the number to ten components to thoroughly dissect the varying components within the signal.
evidence: Description of ICA component selection

claim: The components were thresholded at a z-value ≥1.96 (p-value ≤0.05).
source: The components were thresholded at a z-value ≥1.96 (p-value ≤0.05) (Di and Biswal, 2012), and average z-scores and standard deviations were calculated for each component.
evidence: Description of thresholding method with citation to Di and Biswal, 2012

claim: The Schiffer brain atlas was used to parcelate the brains for ROI seed-based analysis into 23 bilateral regions, the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and the septum (Sep), resulting in a total number of 48 brain regions.
source: The Schiffer brain atlas was used to parcelate the brains for ROI seed-based analysis into 23 bilateral regions, the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and the septum (Sep), resulting in a total number of 48 brain regions.
evidence: Description of brain parcellation method

claim: [11C]DASB was synthesized similarly to the procedure reported by Wilson et al., 2000.
source: [11C]DASB was synthesized similarly to the procedure reported by Wilson et al., 2000.
evidence: Description of radiotracer synthesis with citation to Wilson et al., 2000

claim: A piecewise linear detrend was applied to remove remaining tracer uptake dynamics from the dynamic DVR-1 time series.
source: We applied a piecewise linear detrend to remove remaining tracer uptake dynamics from the dynamic DVR-1 time series and its effect on the artificial inflation of correlation values in the early parts of the scan, before reaching a steady state, while only discarding the first 20 min of every scan, which were too strongly dominated by tracer uptake effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–).
evidence: Description of detrending procedure with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1
